Esteem

ess-TEEM — rhymes with 'A-team'; people hold the A-team in high esteem. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Esteem is deep respect and admiration for someone or something.

The veteran teacher was held in high esteem by students and parents alike.

Worked Example

When the retired coach walks into the gym, the players stop practice just to greet her. The school named its sportsmanship award after her, and former athletes still ask for her advice decades later.

The deep respect and admiration everyone shows her is esteem. Unlike 'fame,' which only means being widely known, esteem is respect that has been earned.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

respect: Respect is admiration for someone's worth — you can respect a stranger's skill after a single meeting. Esteem is respect that has deepened and settled: the lasting high opinion a community holds of someone, usually earned over years of proven character or service.

admiration: Admiration is warm approval and a high opinion, often sparked in a moment by a performance or a brave act. Esteem is steadier and more serious — deep respect earned over time. Admiration can flare up and fade; esteem, once earned, tends to endure.

regard: Regard is consideration and respect, and it is usually the mildest of these words — to be 'held in some regard' is faint praise. Esteem is far stronger: deep respect and admiration, as in 'held in high esteem.' Regard notices a person's worth; esteem honors it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

contempt: the feeling that someone is worthless

disdain: scornful lack of respect

Where it sits · how close to worship it comes — approval → esteem → reverence

approval vs. esteem: Approval is weaker than esteem — approving of someone means you think they did fine, while esteem is deep, lasting respect for who they are.

reverence vs. esteem: Reverence is stronger than esteem: esteem is earned respect, but reverence is awed, almost worshipful respect.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — estim-

root — estim-: to value, to appraise (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin aestimare meant 'to set a value on something.' To hold someone in esteem is literally to appraise them highly — to set a high value on them.

Use the root in a new word: estimate

Use the root in a new word: estimate: The mechanic gave us an estimate of the repair costs before starting work.
